explanations.answer: Paul's teaching and the way he lives
explanations.explanation: Timothy got the front-row seat, friend. Paul says Timothy has observed his teaching and his conduct, and then the list keeps going: purpose, faith, patience, love, perseverance (2 Timothy 3:10). Timothy didn't just hear Paul talk. He watched Paul do it. Anybody can sound good on a Sunday, but it's the Tuesday stuff that shows you.

explanations.answer: Paul's family and the home he keeps
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but Paul never mentions a family or a home in this list. What he says Timothy observed is his teaching, his conduct, his purpose, his faith and more (2 Timothy 3:10). Those are things you can only see by staying close to someone over time. It's a bit like watching how somebody handles a burnt batch instead of touring their kitchen.

explanations.answer: Paul's friends and the money he earns
explanations.explanation: Friends and money aren't on Paul's list, baker. He points to his teaching, his conduct, his purpose, his faith, his patience, his love and his perseverance (2 Timothy 3:10). Not one of those shows up on a paycheck. This list is all about what Timothy saw in Paul himself.

explanations.answer: The Lord rescued him from all of them
explanations.explanation: That's how Paul says it: "Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them." (2 Timothy 3:11) Notice who gets the credit. Paul doesn't say he was tough or clever. He says the Lord rescued him. I think that's a good thing for Timothy to hear before Paul says more about hard times.

explanations.answer: The towns finally welcomed him in
explanations.explanation: Paul never says the towns came around. What he says is that the Lord rescued him from all of those persecutions (2 Timothy 3:11). The rescue came from the Lord, not from a change of heart in Antioch, Iconium or Lystra. Nobody rolled out a welcome mat.

explanations.answer: He learned to stay out of trouble
explanations.explanation: If Paul had a trouble-avoidance plan, he never mentions it. He says, "Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them." (2 Timothy 3:11) The rescue belongs to the Lord, not to Paul's careful planning. And in the very next verse, Paul says all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12), so staying out of trouble isn't the lesson here.

Paul says it straight: "Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted" (2 Timothy 3:12). He just walked through his own stories, so he isn't guessing. It's not exactly a recruiting slogan, is it? But Paul tells Timothy the truth, and it's the same verse that told him the Lord rescued Paul from all of it (2 Timothy 3:11).

Wouldn't that be nice? A round of applause for living godly. But Paul says all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). Timothy had watched Paul's life up close, and it had far more trouble than applause in it. Paul wants him to know that ahead of time.

I would LOVE for this one to be true, friend. A cozy chair, a warm batch, no trouble at all. But Paul says all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). He's honest with Timothy about it, and that honesty is a kindness.

explanations.answer: They go from bad to worse
explanations.explanation: That's the line: "…evil men and imposters go from bad to worse…" (2 Timothy 3:13). An imposter doesn't get better by pretending longer. The direction Paul describes is downhill. It's like a recipe you keep changing without ever checking the dough.

Paul says the opposite, baker. Evil men and imposters "go from bad to worse" (2 Timothy 3:13). Wiser would be going up, and Paul describes going down. Years of faking it didn't turn them into experts.

A confession would be a nice ending, but Paul doesn't describe one. He says evil men and imposters "go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived." (2 Timothy 3:13) That's a road that keeps heading the wrong direction. Nothing in that verse says they stop to come clean.

Close, but Paul says there's a second half. The verse says the imposters go from bad to worse, "deceiving and being deceived." (2 Timothy 3:13) So they fool others, and they get fooled too. Paul says it of them in the same breath.

Right on, because Paul says it goes both ways. Evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, "deceiving and being deceived." (2 Timothy 3:13) They're fooling others while getting fooled themselves. That's one tangled mess, and Paul says it plainly.

explanations.answer: Continue in what he has learned
explanations.explanation: That's it: "But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed…" (2 Timothy 3:14). Imposters are going from bad to worse, and Paul's answer isn't to chase something new. It's to keep going in what Timothy already learned and firmly believed. Steady wins here.

explanations.answer: Look for a fresh new teaching
explanations.explanation: Paul sends Timothy the other way, friend. He says, "But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed…" (2 Timothy 3:14). With imposters around, a shiny new teaching isn't the plan. Timothy already has what he needs, so he's told to stay with it.

Paul doesn't tell Timothy to hide and wait it out. He says, "But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed…" (2 Timothy 3:14). Continuing is an active word, not a sit-still word. Timothy keeps going while the imposters keep going downhill.

explanations.answer: He knows who he learned them from
explanations.explanation: Paul gives the reason right in the verse: "…since you know from whom you have learned them." (2 Timothy 3:14) Timothy knows the people he learned from. Paul doesn't say who here, so I won't guess past the text. What matters is that Timothy knows the source and can trust it.

Paul never brings up a headcount. His reason is, "…since you know from whom you have learned them." (2 Timothy 3:14) And with imposters deceiving and being deceived in the verse before, a crowd isn't the thing to lean on. Timothy leans on who taught him.

explanations.answer: He worked them out on his own
explanations.explanation: Timothy wasn't a lone genius in a kitchen, baker. Paul says, "…since you know from whom you have learned them." (2 Timothy 3:14) Learned from someone, not invented alone. That's the reason Paul gives, and it makes Timothy's footing solid.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures…" (2 Timothy 3:15). That's long before Timothy ever met Paul. Timothy's roots in the Word go back to when he was a baby.

You got it. Paul says, "From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures…" (2 Timothy 3:15). So Timothy knew them well before he met Paul. Paul wasn't introducing him to the Word. He was reminding him of what he already had.

Yes, faith. Paul says the Holy Scriptures "are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." (2 Timothy 3:15) The Scriptures lead to wisdom, and that wisdom comes through faith in Christ Jesus. It's a short word carrying a big load.

Good effort, but Paul says "faith," not works. The Scriptures "are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." (2 Timothy 3:15) Faith in Christ Jesus is where the wisdom lands. No scorecard in that verse.

Paul doesn't use that word here, baker. He says the Holy Scriptures "are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." (2 Timothy 3:15) The word is faith, and it's in Christ Jesus. Rituals never come up.

That's what "God-breathed" means: "All Scripture is God-breathed…" (2 Timothy 3:16). The source is God Himself. It's not a collection of good ideas somebody had. Paul puts the word ALL in front of Scripture, too.

Paul points higher than that. He says, "All Scripture is God-breathed…" (2 Timothy 3:16). God is the source, not a line of elders. People did hand down what they'd received in many places, but that's not what this verse says. This verse says it came from God's breath.
No committee meeting here, friend. Paul says, "All Scripture is God-breathed…" (2 Timothy 3:16). The source is God, and Paul includes ALL Scripture. Nobody gets the credit that belongs to Him.

Yes, correction is on Paul's list. Scripture "is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16). It's one of four uses. Correction isn't fun in the moment, but Paul says it's useful, and I'm not going to argue with him.

It's actually on the list, baker. Paul says Scripture "is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16). Correction sits right there with the other three. Scripture is useful for it, so this one is true.

explanations.answer: Equipping the man of God for every good work
explanations.explanation: That's the goal: "…so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work." (2 Timothy 3:17) All four uses lead there. Complete, fully equipped, and ready for every good work. Nothing missing from the toolbox.

explanations.answer: Helping the man of God win every argument
explanations.explanation: Arguments never come up in Paul's goal, friend. He says it's "…so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work." (2 Timothy 3:17) The point is good work, not winning. A trophy shelf for debates isn't mentioned anywhere.

explanations.answer: Keeping the man of God safe from all hardship
explanations.explanation: Paul already told Timothy the opposite earlier in the passage. All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). So the goal here isn't a hardship-free life. It's "…so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work." (2 Timothy 3:17)
